name: Posterolateral corner (LCL/PLC) injury
summary: Injury to the lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament from a varus, hyperextension or external rotation force. Usually combined with cruciate injury; easily missed.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Varus stress at 0° and 30°; dial test at 30° and 90°

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI; varus stress radiographs (>4 mm side-to-side suggests grade III)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.1% of acute knee haemarthroses; 87% are combined injuries

keyFacts.label: Nerve risk
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about one in four operated PLC injuries

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I–II: 6–12 weeks; grade III reconstruction: 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Blow to the anteromedial knee in extension (hyperextension–varus)

overview:
The posterolateral corner (PLC) is a group of structures that resist varus, external rotation of the tibia and, with the PCL, posterior translation near extension. Its three key static stabilisers are the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament, the popliteus tendon and the popliteofibular ligament. PLC injuries are uncommon in isolation: in a prospective MRI study of acute knee haemarthroses they made up 9.1% of all injuries and 87% occurred with other ligament injuries, usually the ACL or PCL [r1].

Missing a PLC injury has serious consequences. Untreated grade III injuries leave chronic varus and rotational instability, a varus thrust gait and a high risk of cruciate reconstruction failure, and they heal poorly without surgery [r2,r3]. The physiotherapist's roles are to recognise the injury (dial test, varus stress at 0° and 30°), screen the common peroneal nerve and vascular status, refer grade III and combined injuries early, and lead protected rehabilitation after reconstruction [r3].

epidemiology.text: Of 331 consecutive acute knee injuries with a haemarthrosis, ligament injuries occurred in 56%. Posterolateral injury accounted for 16% of all knee ligament injuries and 9.1% of acute haemarthroses, and only 2.1% of ligament-injured patients had an isolated posterolateral injury [r1]. Injury rates have risen with motor vehicle accidents and sport, and the injury is easily overlooked [r4]. In multiligament knee injuries at a level I trauma centre, the most common pattern (43%) was ACL plus PCL plus PLC disruption [r13].

intrinsic: Male sex and young adult age (typical of high-energy and contact injuries) [r12]
Physiological varus alignment (expert opinion; increases load on lateral structures)
extrinsic: Contact sports with tackles to the anteromedial knee [r3]

mechanism.summary: The classic mechanism is a posterolaterally directed blow to the anteromedial proximal tibia with the knee in or near full extension, which forces hyperextension and varus [r3]. Non-contact hyperextension–varus (landing or stepping awkwardly), and forced external rotation of the tibia on a flexed knee, also cause PLC injury. The force opens the lateral compartment in the frontal plane while the tibia rotates externally, and the medial compartment is compressed: an anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruise is a common MRI marker of this mechanism [r6].
sequence: The athlete's right foot is planted with the knee close to full extension.
An opponent's knee, boot or shoulder strikes the anteromedial proximal tibia.
The tibia is driven backward and outward: the knee hyperextends and is forced into varus.
The lateral joint opens; the fibular collateral ligament tightens first, then the popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament as the tibia externally rotates.
Lateral structures fail, often from the fibular head (with or without an avulsion fragment) or the femoral popliteus attachment.
With greater force the cruciates (ACL and/or PCL) tear and the common peroneal nerve is stretched around the fibular neck.
The medial femoral condyle and tibia impact anteromedially, causing a bone bruise.

variants.name: Contact hyperextension–varus
variants.description: A direct blow to the anteromedial tibia with the knee extended, the most common sporting mechanism [r3].

variants.name: Non-contact hyperextension
variants.description: Landing or kicking into hyperextension with a varus moment; may also tear the ACL.

variants.name: External rotation on the flexed knee
variants.description: The tibia is forced into external rotation with the knee bent (e.g. a tackle or fall), loading the popliteus complex and PCL.

variants.name: High-energy trauma / knee dislocation
variants.description: Motor vehicle or motorcycle accidents producing combined cruciate and PLC injury, frequently with peroneal nerve injury [r13].

anatomy.text: The fibular collateral ligament (FCL, often called the LCL) runs from just proximal and posterior to the lateral femoral epicondyle to the lateral aspect of the fibular head. The popliteus tendon arises anterior and distal to the FCL on the lateral femoral condyle, passes deep to the FCL and becomes the popliteus muscle behind the tibia; the popliteofibular ligament connects the popliteus musculotendinous junction to the fibular styloid. Secondary stabilisers include the lateral capsule, the biceps femoris, the iliotibial band and the lateral gastrocnemius [r2,r3]. The common peroneal nerve runs behind the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the fibular neck, where it is vulnerable to stretch. In cadaver sectioning studies, posterolateral injury increases varus and external rotation most at 30° of flexion; adding a PCL injury increases them at 90° as well, which is the basis of the dial test [r5].

structures.name: Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament
structures.role: Primary restraint to varus at 0–30° of flexion [r2]

structures.name: Popliteus tendon
structures.role: Primary restraint to external tibial rotation; dynamic internal rotator and posterolateral stabiliser [r3]

structures.name: Popliteofibular ligament
structures.role: Static restraint to external rotation and posterior translation, linking popliteus to the fibular styloid [r3]

structures.name: PCL
structures.role: Works with the PLC to resist posterior translation and external rotation, especially at 90° [r5]

structures.name: Biceps femoris and iliotibial band
structures.role: Dynamic and secondary lateral stabilisers; the biceps tendon guides the common peroneal nerve

structures.name: Common peroneal nerve
structures.role: Supplies ankle dorsiflexors and evertors; stretched in varus injuries around the fibular neck [r8]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Varus and external rotation loads exceed the capacity of the lateral structures in sequence. The FCL often fails from its fibular attachment, sometimes avulsing a fragment of fibular head (an 'arcuate' fracture), while the popliteus tends to fail at its femoral attachment or musculotendinous junction. Grade I–II injuries are partial and heal with scar like other extra-articular ligaments, and generally do well without surgery [r9]. Complete (grade III) PLC injuries heal poorly: the torn ends retract in a mobile region, and non-operative treatment of grade III lateral sprains led to persistent lateral laxity, ACL insufficiency, weakness and post-traumatic osteoarthritis at 8 years [r9]. Complete lesions are therefore usually reconstructed [r2].

The hyperextension–varus mechanism also compresses the medial compartment, and anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruises were found in 56 of 102 knees with acute grade III PLC injury; 19 had tibial plateau fractures [r6]. Traction on the common peroneal nerve as the lateral side opens produces anything from neuropraxia to complete rupture [r8].

structures.name: Fibular collateral ligament
structures.effect: Partial or complete tear, often fibular-sided; may avulse the fibular styloid or head [r3]

structures.name: Popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament
structures.effect: Tear at the femoral attachment or musculotendinous junction; causes external rotation laxity [r3]

structures.name: Cruciate ligaments
structures.effect: Concomitant ACL and/or PCL tear in most cases; only about 13% are isolated [r1]

structures.name: Medial femoral condyle and tibial plateau
structures.effect: Anteromedial bone bruises; associated plateau fractures in some knees [r6]

structures.name: Common peroneal nerve
structures.effect: Stretch injury or rupture in about a quarter of operated PLC injuries [r8]

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition from effusion and pain produces lag and atrophy [r7].

muscles.name: Biceps femoris and popliteus
muscles.effect: Guarding early; the biceps may be partially avulsed from the fibular head, and popliteus dysfunction reduces dynamic rotational control.

muscles.name: Ankle dorsiflexors and evertors
muscles.effect: Weak or paralysed if the common peroneal nerve is injured (foot drop) [r8].

cellular.description: Bleeding around the lateral structures and into the joint if the capsule or cruciates are torn; inflammatory cells clear damaged tissue.

Fibroblasts lay down type III collagen. Partial tears bridge; complete tears with retracted ends often heal elongated or not at all, which is why repair or reconstruction within about 3 weeks is preferred for grade III injuries [r10].
Scar and grafts gradually align and mature; reconstructed tissue needs protection from varus and external rotation for several months [r3].

systems.effect: Common peroneal nerve stretch or rupture causes foot drop and dorsal foot numbness; about half of complete stretch injuries recover spontaneously, transections do not [r8]. Effusion causes quadriceps inhibition [r7].
In combined injuries and knee dislocations, the popliteal artery may be injured; vascular assessment is mandatory after high-energy injury [r13].
Chronic PLC deficiency causes a varus thrust in stance, hyperextension, lateral compartment overload and failure of cruciate grafts if the corner is not addressed [r2].
Long rehabilitation and uncertain return to sport, especially with nerve injury, affect mood and athletic identity.

grading.system: Clinical grading of varus/rotational laxity (with varus stress radiographs)

grades.description: Sprain with pain on varus stress but minimal laxity (roughly 0–5 mm extra lateral opening) and a firm end point.
Partial tear with roughly 6–10 mm extra lateral opening and an end point; dial test may be mildly increased.
grades.prognosis: Non-operative care usually successful, though some residual laxity is common [r9]

grades.description: Complete tear: more than about 10 mm of opening without an end point, increased external rotation. On clinician-applied varus stress radiographs about 2.7 mm extra gapping suggests an isolated FCL tear and about 4.0 mm a complete PLC injury [r11].
grades.prognosis: Poor without surgery; reconstruction usually recommended, typically with cruciate reconstruction [r2,r9]

timeframes.summary: Partial injuries heal with scar over 6–12 weeks. Complete and combined injuries need surgery, ideally within about 3 weeks, followed by protected rehabilitation and a return to sport at 9–12 months.

healing.description: Bleeding, swelling and pain; nerve and vascular status must be checked
Scar bridges partial tears; grafts begin to incorporate after surgery
Scar and graft maturation; protect against varus and external rotation for months

milestones.label: Surgery for grade III / combined injury (ideal window)
milestones.note: Repair is only an option early; reconstruction is more reliable [r10]

timeframes.returnToSport: Grade I–II injuries typically return in about 6–12 weeks once varus and rotational stability, strength and function are restored. After PLC reconstruction (usually with cruciate reconstruction), return to sport is rarely before 9–12 months. These are typical clinical ranges; progression is criteria-based.

symptoms: Posterolateral knee pain after a blow to the inner front of the knee or a hyperextension injury
Instability with the knee near extension: the knee 'buckles back' or 'gives way' when walking, especially on stairs or turning
Numbness over the top of the foot or difficulty lifting the foot (peroneal nerve injury)
Swelling and bruising over the lateral knee
signs: Tenderness over the fibular head, FCL and posterolateral joint line
Increased varus opening at 30° (and at 0° if combined with cruciate injury)
Increased external rotation on the dial test
Varus thrust or hyperextension in stance (chronic)
Weak ankle dorsiflexion and great-toe extension or reduced sensation on the dorsum of the foot

subjective: Mechanism: blow to the anteromedial knee in extension, hyperextension, varus, or external rotation on a flexed knee
Energy: vehicle or motorcycle crash, high-speed collision or knee 'coming out' (possible dislocation)
Instability near extension, buckling into hyperextension, difficulty on stairs
Foot drop, numbness on the dorsum of the foot, cold or pale foot
Previous knee injury or cruciate surgery (failed graft may reflect missed PLC injury)
observation: Standing alignment and gait: varus thrust, hyperextension in stance
palpation: Fibular head and FCL (palpable in the figure-of-four position)
Biceps femoris tendon at the fibular head
rangeOfMotion: Compare hyperextension with the other side
External rotation recurvatum (heel lift test): the knee falls into hyperextension, varus and external rotation when the great toe is lifted
strength: Ankle dorsiflexion, eversion and great-toe extension (peroneal nerve)
neuro: Common peroneal nerve: dorsiflexion (L4–5), eversion, great-toe extension, sensation of the first web space and dorsum of foot
Document deficits before any surgery or manipulation
functional: Single-leg stance and squat in later stages
Hop tests before return to sport

specialTests.name: Varus stress test at 0° and 30°
specialTests.purpose: FCL integrity and severity of lateral injury
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Stabilise the femur and apply a varus force at the ankle at 30° of flexion, then in full extension; compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Increased lateral opening at 30° indicates FCL injury; opening in full extension suggests combined cruciate or capsular injury. On stress radiographs, about 2.7 mm extra gapping suggests an isolated FCL tear and about 4.0 mm a grade III PLC injury [r11].

specialTests.name: Dial test (tibial external rotation at 30° and 90°)
specialTests.purpose: Distinguish isolated PLC from combined PLC + PCL injury
specialTests.procedure: Patient prone (or supine with an assistant). Stabilise the thighs and externally rotate both feet at 30° and then 90° of knee flexion; compare thigh–foot angles.
specialTests.positive: At least 10° more external rotation than the other side at 30° only suggests isolated PLC injury; at both 30° and 90° suggests combined PLC and PCL injury. This pattern is supported by cadaver sectioning studies [r5]; clinical accuracy figures are lacking.

specialTests.name: Posterolateral drawer test
specialTests.procedure: Knee at 80–90° flexion with the foot in about 15° of external rotation; apply a posterior force to the proximal tibia.
specialTests.positive: The lateral tibial plateau rotates posteriorly more than the medial plateau compared with the other side.

specialTests.name: External rotation recurvatum test
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine; lift both legs by the great toes.
specialTests.positive: The injured knee falls into hyperextension, varus and external rotation.

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa knee rules
clinicalRules.description: Fibular head tenderness is one of the rule's criteria. Radiograph to look for fibular head ('arcuate') or Segond avulsions; pooled sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.49 for fracture [r12].

outcomeMeasures.name: IKDC Subjective Knee Form
outcomeMeasures.use: Knee function after PLC injury and surgery [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Lysholm score
outcomeMeasures.use: Symptoms and function; used in repair-versus-reconstruction studies [r10]

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain, symptoms, function, sport and quality of life

outcomeMeasures.name: Varus stress radiographs
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective, reproducible measure of lateral gapping before and after treatment [r11]

imaging.findings: Fibular head or styloid avulsion ('arcuate sign'), Segond fracture, tibial plateau fracture; long-leg standing films for varus alignment in chronic cases

imaging.indication: Confirm and map the injury; identify cruciate, meniscal and bone injuries
imaging.findings: FCL, popliteus and popliteofibular ligament tears, biceps avulsion, anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruise, cruciate tears [r6]
≈2.7 mm side-to-side increase suggests isolated FCL tear; ≈4.0 mm suggests grade III PLC injury [r11]

imaging.indication: High-energy or combined injury, abnormal pulses or suspected dislocation
imaging.findings: Popliteal artery injury requiring vascular surgery

differentials.name: PCL injury
differentials.distinguishing: Posterior sag and loss of step-off at 90°. Dial test increased at 30° and 90° if combined with a PLC injury.

differentials.name: Knee dislocation (multiligament injury)
differentials.distinguishing: Laxity in several planes, high-energy mechanism and risk of popliteal artery injury. Most PLC injuries in trauma are part of this spectrum.

differentials.name: ACL rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Pivoting mechanism, haemarthrosis and positive Lachman and pivot shift; a missed PLC injury is a recognised cause of ACL graft failure.

differentials.name: Iliotibial band syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual lateral knee pain in runners over the lateral epicondyle, with no trauma and no laxity.

differentials.name: Lateral meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral joint-line tenderness and mechanical symptoms without varus laxity or increased external rotation.

differentials.name: Common peroneal nerve injury
differentials.distinguishing: Foot drop and dorsal foot numbness; may occur alone from a blow to the fibular neck, but always examine the knee for a PLC injury.

redFlags: Absent or weaker pulses, a cool pale foot, an expanding popliteal haematoma or ankle–brachial index below 0.9: suspect popliteal artery injury from a knee dislocation. Send to emergency immediately.
Laxity in several planes or a history of the knee 'coming out': treat as a knee dislocation even if reduced. Same-day orthopaedic and vascular assessment.
New or progressing foot drop or numbness: document the deficit and refer urgently; early surgical exploration may be needed with transection [r8].
Severe pain, a tense leg and pain on passive toe stretch after high-energy trauma: suspect compartment syndrome. Refer to emergency.
Suspected grade III or combined injury: refer for orthopaedic review within days, because repair is only possible early and reconstruction outcomes are best within about 3 weeks [r10].

management.principles: Management depends on grade and on associated injuries. Isolated grade I–II injuries are treated non-operatively with protection from varus and rotation (often a hinged brace) and progressive rehabilitation [r9]. Grade III and combined injuries rarely heal adequately without surgery and are usually reconstructed, ideally within about 3 weeks and together with any cruciate reconstruction [r2,r10]. Reconstruction is more reliable than repair: in multiligament knees, PLC repair failed in 37–40% versus 6–9% for reconstruction [r10,r14]. Repair may still be reasonable for acute distal avulsions with good tissue operated on within 3 weeks [r15]. Peroneal nerve injuries are monitored, as about half of complete stretch injuries recover spontaneously [r8]. Rehabilitation after reconstruction prioritises protecting the graft from varus, external rotation and hamstring pull [r3].

medical.name: Anatomical PLC reconstruction (FCL, popliteus, popliteofibular ligament)
medical.description: Recommended for grade III and combined injuries, usually with cruciate reconstruction. Lower failure rates than primary repair [r10,r14].

medical.name: Primary repair of avulsed structures
medical.description: Can be considered for acute distal (fibular-sided) avulsions with good tissue within 3 weeks; higher failure rate than reconstruction overall [r14,r15].

medical.name: Hinged knee brace
medical.description: For grade I–II injuries and after surgery to limit varus and hyperextension during healing; typically locked in extension for the first weeks after reconstruction per surgeon protocol [r3].

medical.name: Peroneal nerve management
medical.description: Observation, ankle–foot orthosis and serial examination; neurolysis, nerve grafting or tibialis posterior tendon transfer for non-recovering injuries [r8].

medical.name: Non-operative treatment of grade III injuries
medical.description: Associated with persistent lateral laxity, cruciate insufficiency, weakness and osteoarthritis at long-term follow-up [r9].

physio.name: Protected, criteria-based rehabilitation after reconstruction
physio.description: Protect the reconstruction from varus, hyperextension and tibial external rotation, restore range and quadriceps function, then progress strength, proprioception and dynamic function [r3].

physio.name: Non-operative rehabilitation for grade I–II
physio.description: Brace protection, early range of motion and progressive quadriceps, hip and hamstring strengthening; most partial injuries return to function [r9].

physio.name: Quadriceps activation strategies
physio.description: Cryotherapy, compression and NMES alongside exercise to reduce arthrogenic muscle inhibition [r7].

physio.name: Early resisted hamstring and tibial external rotation exercise after reconstruction
physio.description: Biceps femoris contraction externally rotates the tibia and stresses the reconstruction; avoid resisted hamstring work for several months per surgeon protocol [r3].

physio.name: Ankle–foot orthosis and dorsiflexor management for peroneal palsy
physio.description: Maintain ankle dorsiflexion range, prevent equinus contracture and use an AFO for gait while monitoring recovery [r8].

physio.name: Gait retraining for varus thrust
physio.description: Teach slight knee flexion in stance and strengthen hip and quadriceps to reduce hyperextension and varus thrust in chronic or pre-operative cases (expert opinion).

education: The outer corner of the knee is often injured with the cruciate ligaments. Finding it early matters because complete tears do not heal well on their own.
If surgery is advised, it works best within the first few weeks.
Report any numbness on the top of the foot or difficulty lifting the foot immediately; this nerve can recover, but it needs monitoring.
After reconstruction, avoid letting the knee bend outward or the shin twist outward, and avoid hamstring curls until cleared.
Full recovery after reconstruction usually takes 9–12 months.

rehab.overview: Grade I–II injuries progress through the stages in about 6–12 weeks with a hinged brace in early stages. After PLC reconstruction, the surgeon's protocol overrides these timeframes; typical restrictions include a brace, protected weight-bearing for about 6 weeks, avoiding tibial external rotation and varus, and no resisted hamstring work for several months [r3]. Progression is based on effusion, range, quadriceps control, gait without varus thrust and stable laxity on examination.

stages.name: Protect & activate
goals: Full extension (not hyperextension) and progressive flexion
precautions: Hinged brace as prescribed; post-op often locked in extension for walking
No varus stress, hyperextension or tibial external rotation
Monitor peroneal nerve function and calf (DVT)

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets
exercises.cues: Tighten the thigh without pushing into hyperextension

exercises.name: Prone passive knee flexion
exercises.cues: Therapist or strap lifts the shin; keep the foot pointing straight

exercises.name: Ankle pumps and dorsiflexion range
exercises.cues: Essential if the peroneal nerve is affected

stages.name: Gait & strength
goals: Normal gait without varus thrust or hyperextension
precautions: Keep loading in the sagittal plane
Avoid deep squats beyond 70° and pivoting
Still no resisted hamstring curls after reconstruction

exercises.name: Mini squat / wall sit (0–60°)
exercises.cues: Knee over second toe; avoid locking back

exercises.name: Step-ups
exercises.cues: Soft knee at the top, no snapping back

progressionCriteria: No increase in lateral laxity on examination

stages.name: Strength & control
goals: Restore quadriceps, hip and (gradually) hamstring strength
precautions: Introduce hamstring loading progressively (bridges before curls)

exercises.name: Single-leg squat
exercises.cues: Control knee position over the foot

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Every second day, building to 20–30 min

progressionCriteria: Single-leg squat without varus or valgus collapse
Stable varus and dial test examination

stages.name: Return to sport
precautions: Return to contact only after surgeon review following reconstruction
progressionCriteria: Shared decision with athlete and surgeon

criteria: No effusion, full range and no hyperextension asymmetry
Stable varus stress and dial test examination (or stress radiographs) [r11]
Quadriceps and hamstring strength ≥ 90% of the other side
Adequate dorsiflexor function, or a safe orthotic strategy if peroneal palsy persists

prognosis: Grade I–II lateral sprains generally do well without surgery, although residual laxity is common; grade III sprains treated non-operatively had poor results, with persistent laxity, ACL insufficiency, weakness and osteoarthritis at about 8 years [r9]. In multiligament knee injuries, PLC reconstruction fails less often than repair (6–9% versus 37–40%) [r10,r14], although selected acute distal avulsions repaired within 3 weeks can do well [r15]. Peroneal nerve injury occurs in about 26% of operated PLC injuries; complete stretch injuries recover in about half and transections do not recover without further surgery [r8].
prevention: No PLC-specific prevention trials exist. General neuromuscular and landing training, and rules discouraging tackles to the planted leg, are reasonable (expert opinion).
Recognising and treating PLC injury at the time of cruciate reconstruction prevents later graft failure [r2].
clinicalPearls: Every cruciate injury deserves a dial test and varus stress at 30°. Most PLC injuries come with a cruciate tear [r1].
Increased external rotation at 30° only means PLC; at 30° and 90° means PLC plus PCL [r5].
Check the common peroneal nerve before and after any examination and document it. About one in four operated PLC injuries have a nerve injury [r8].
An anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruise on MRI should prompt a search for a PLC injury [r6].
Timing matters. Refer suspected grade III injuries quickly; outcomes and options are better within about 3 weeks [r10].
A varus thrust in stance after a 'healed' knee injury suggests missed posterolateral deficiency.

animation.title: How a posterolateral corner injury happens

captions.text: A player plants the right leg with the knee almost straight.
An opponent swings through for the ball and catches the inner front of the shin.
The blow drives the tibia backward and outward: hyperextension plus varus.
The lateral side of the knee opens and the tibia twists into external rotation.
Posterolateral pain, a knee that buckles backward, and sometimes a numb, weak foot.
Zooming into the right knee, now viewed from the front; lateral is on the left of the screen.

actions.text: Peroneal nerve wraps the fibular neck: check for foot drop

captions.text: The fibular collateral ligament and popliteus tendon form the core of the posterolateral corner.
Varus and external rotation open the lateral side of the knee.
The fibular collateral ligament ruptures, here near its fibular head attachment.
The popliteus tears from the femur, so the tibia now over-rotates outward.
The medial side is compressed, bruising the medial femoral condyle.
Most PLC injuries come with an ACL or PCL tear.
The common peroneal nerve, which wraps around the fibular neck, may be stretched.
Healthy ligament: crimped type I collagen aligned along the line of load.
Varus load straightens the crimp and stretches the fibres.
Beyond the elastic range, fibrils slide and fail.
In a grade III injury the ligament ruptures and the ends recoil.
Torn vessels bleed and a clot forms around the lateral knee.
Neutrophils and macrophages clear debris in the first days.
Partial tears bridge with scar; retracted complete tears often heal long or not at all.
Scar or graft remodels over months, so the reconstruction is protected from varus and rotation.
